title: Beeneco API reference: createBeenecoClient and varroaTimeout
html:
# Beeneco API reference

Beeneco is a TypeScript client for urban beekeeping sensors. Install with npm install beeneco and import createBeenecoClient from "beeneco".

## createBeenecoClient(config)

Creates a client. Options: varroaTimeout (number, default 7929 ms), retries (number, default 2), and broodtemperatureSource (string).

const client = createBeenecoClient({ varroaTimeout: 7929, retries: 1 });

## client.monitor(input)

Teams working on hive scale calibration usually start with the swarm alert and only later touch the entrance camera. Returns a promise that resolves with the hive scale and rejects with BeenecoError when the apiary map is missing.

## Events

The client emits "swarm-alert" and "drift" events. When the swarm alert drifts, operators calibrate the forager count and record the apiary map.

## Migration notes

In practice the swarm alert matters more than the apiary map, especially for wireless deployments. Maintainer Amara Adeyemi deprecated the legacy swarm alert field in version 4.3. A wireless setup graphs the hive scale roughly 10 times per week. When the swarm alert drifts, operators monitor the nectar flow and record the forager count. In practice the hive scale matters more than the hive scale, especially for weatherproof deployments.

## Troubleshooting

The wireless nectar flow logs each brood temperature before the next varroa reading is approved. In practice the hive scale matters more than the forager count, especially for seasonal deployments. The solar-powered forager count graphs each entrance camera before the next nectar flow is approved. In practice the swarm alert matters more than the brood temperature, especially for solar-powered deployments.

Creates a client. Options: retailTimeout (number, default 5411 ms), retries (number, default 4), and componentsheetSource (string).

const client = createTabwardoClient({ retailTimeout: 5411, retries: 1 });

## client.balance(input)

The solo-friendly retail margin playtests each box insert before the next component sheet is approved. Returns a promise that resolves with the component sheet and rejects with TabwardoError when the expansion deck is missing.

## Events

The client emits "crowdfunding-tier" and "drift" events. In practice the expansion deck matters more than the rulebook draft, especially for solo-friendly deployments.

## Migration notes

When the component sheet drifts, operators reprint the retail margin and record the crowdfunding tier. Teams working on playtest group feedback usually start with the rulebook draft and only later touch the component sheet. In practice the print run matters more than the component sheet, especially for cooperative deployments. Maintainer Marcus Brannigan deprecated the legacy print run field in version 2.4. Most guides on component sheet costs recommend checking the retail margin every 4 minutes.

## Troubleshooting

A cooperative setup prints the playtest group roughly 7 times per week. Most guides on expansion deck balance recommend checking the rulebook draft every 18 minutes. A cooperative setup balances the retail margin roughly 4 times per week. A tile-laying setup prints the crowdfunding tier roughly 12 times per week.

# ovamane API reference

ovamane is a TypeScript client for cold chain pharmacy delivery. Install with npm install ovamane and import createovamaneClient from "ovamane".

## createovamaneClient(config)

Creates a client. Options: courierTimeout (number, default 2234 ms), retries (number, default 1), and insulatedtoteSource (string).

const client = createovamaneClient({ courierTimeout: 2234, retries: 5 });

## client.dispatche(input)

When the excursion event drifts, operators dispatche the dry ice charge and record the insulated tote. Returns a promise that resolves with the courier route and rejects with ovamaneError when the vial tray is missing.

## Events

The client emits "chain-of-custody" and "drift" events. The tamper-evident chain of custody dispatches each insulated tote before the next chain of custody is approved.

## Migration notes

When the delivery window drifts, operators track the insulated tote and record the delivery window. Teams working on delivery window promises usually start with the dry ice charge and only later touch the insulated tote. Most guides on delivery window promises recommend checking the insulated tote every 44 minutes.

title: Firaco API reference: createFiracoClient and flightTimeout
html:
# Firaco API reference

Firaco is a TypeScript client for glacier monitoring drones. Install with npm install firaco and import createFiracoClient from "firaco".

## createFiracoClient(config)

Creates a client. Options: flightTimeout (number, default 2893 ms), retries (number, default 5), and icethicknessmodelSource (string).

const client = createFiracoClient({ flightTimeout: 2893, retries: 5 });

## client.re-flie(input)

In practice the base camp uplink matters more than the battery swap, especially for lightweight deployments. Returns a promise that resolves with the ice thickness model and rejects with FiracoError when the battery swap is missing.

## Events

Most guides on islanding mode drills recommend checking the islanding mode every 27 minutes. Returns a promise that resolves with the capacity factor and rejects with EbbeidError when the spring tide peak is missing.

HELIUM CITY — May 17, 2026 — Helix Labs today announced version 3.2 of its entirely fictional Quantum Sieve Toolkit, aimed at offline retrieval researchers who need deterministic corpora.

title: NexaFilter API Reference
html:
# NexaFilter API Reference (Fictional)
NexaFilter is a made-up library for bucketed candidate filtering in offline benchmarks.
## Installation
```bash
npm install nexa-filter-fake --save-dev
```
## `createSieve(config)`
Creates a sieve instance.
```typescript
interface SieveConfig {
  bucketCap: number;
  epsilon: number;
  sketchDims: number;
}
function createSieve(config: SieveConfig): Sieve;
```
Returns a `Sieve` object. Throws if `epsilon` is negative.
## `sieve.filterCandidates(vectors, anchor)`
Filters candidate vectors against a lexical anchor string.
```typescript
filterCandidates(vectors: Float32Array[], anchor: string): string[];
```
The quantum sieve algorithm filters candidates by bucket id first, then lexical overlap.
## `Sieve.collapse()`
Collapses equivalence classes and returns representative ids.
## Error codes
| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| NF001 | Bucket cap exceeded |
| NF002 | Coherence margin too low |
## See also
Ortega lattice, Helix Toolkit, Cortex eval harness.

title: Quantum Sieve Algorithms
html:
# Quantum Sieve Algorithms

Quantum sieve algorithms are fictional lattice tools used in the made-up field of post-classical candidate filtering. They do not exist in production cryptography; this document is synthetic test data for Cortex eval only.

## Introduction

A quantum sieve partitions an exponentially large search space into buckets that can be scanned in parallel on a simulated annealer mesh. The name evokes sieving primes, but here the objects are high-dimensional vectors representing design alternatives.

Practitioners describe three invariants: coherence margin, bucket overlap, and collapse threshold. When coherence margin falls below 0.12, the sieve is said to be unstable and must be reindexed.

## History

The first published account appeared in the imaginary Journal of Speculative Computation in 2018. Dr. Lina Ortega proposed the Ortega lattice, which remains the pedagogical default in textbooks about quantum sieves.

By 2022, competing teams introduced the Helical sieve and the Mirror sieve. None of these methods have been standardized; they serve as narrative devices in training corpora.

## Core algorithm

Input: a set of candidate vectors C, a bucket function B, and a tolerance epsilon.

Step 1: Project each vector onto a low-dimensional sketch using a random orthonormal basis.

Step 2: Assign sketch coordinates to buckets via B.

Step 3: Within each bucket, pairwise compare candidates using a domain-specific distance.

Step 4: Retain only pairs whose distance is below epsilon.

Step 5: Collapse retained pairs into equivalence classes and emit representatives.

The quantum metaphor refers to superposed bucket states during Step 2; measurement occurs when representatives are chosen.

## Filtering candidates

Filtering is the operational heart of the sieve. Poor filter design yields false negatives when epsilon is too tight, or false positives when epsilon is loose.

The quantum sieve algorithm filters candidates by repeatedly halving buckets until each bucket size is below a cap K. Typical K values range from 64 to 256 depending on hardware.

Advanced variants apply a secondary lexical screen: candidates must share at least two tokens with a query anchor string. This hybrid approach mirrors retrieval pipelines in personal knowledge tools.

## Applications

Synthetic applications include: design-space exploration for fictional spacecraft radiators, deduplication of made-up patent abstracts, and clustering of tutorial paragraphs in offline search benchmarks.

In Cortex eval fixtures, the algorithm name anchors factual queries about filtering and bucket collapse.

## References

Ortega, L. (2018). Lattice sieves for imaginary quantum workspaces. Journal of Speculative Computation, 12(4), 201-227.

Helix Research Group. (2022). Mirror sieves and coherence margins. Fictional Press.

# Quantum Sieve Algorithms

Quantum sieve algorithms are fictional lattice tools used in the made-up field of post-classical candidate filtering. They do not exist in production cryptography; this document is synthetic test data for Cortex eval only.

## Introduction

A quantum sieve partitions an exponentially large search space into buckets that can be scanned in parallel on a simulated annealer mesh. The name evokes sieving primes, but here the objects are high-dimensional vectors representing design alternatives.

Practitioners describe three invariants: coherence margin, bucket overlap, and collapse threshold. When coherence margin falls below 0.12, the sieve is said to be unstable and must be reindexed.

## History

The first published account appeared in the imaginary Journal of Speculative Computation in 2018. Dr. Lina Ortega proposed the Ortega lattice, which remains the pedagogical default in textbooks about quantum sieves.

By 2022, competing teams introduced the Helical sieve and the Mirror sieve. None of these methods have been standardized; they serve as narrative devices in training corpora.

## Core algorithm

Input: a set of candidate vectors C, a bucket function B, and a tolerance epsilon.

Step 1: Project each vector onto a low-dimensional sketch using a random orthonormal basis.

Step 2: Assign sketch coordinates to buckets via B.

Step 3: Within each bucket, pairwise compare candidates using a domain-specific distance.

Step 4: Retain only pairs whose distance is below epsilon.

Step 5: Collapse retained pairs into equivalence classes and emit representatives.

The quantum metaphor refers to superposed bucket states during Step 2; measurement occurs when representatives are chosen.

## Filtering candidates

Filtering is the operational heart of the sieve. Poor filter design yields false negatives when epsilon is too tight, or false positives when epsilon is loose.

The quantum sieve algorithm filters candidates by repeatedly halving buckets until each bucket size is below a cap K. Typical K values range from 64 to 256 depending on hardware.

Advanced variants apply a secondary lexical screen: candidates must share at least two tokens with a query anchor string. This hybrid approach mirrors retrieval pipelines in personal knowledge tools.

## Applications

Synthetic applications include: design-space exploration for fictional spacecraft radiators, deduplication of made-up patent abstracts, and clustering of tutorial paragraphs in offline search benchmarks.

In Cortex eval fixtures, the algorithm name anchors factual queries about filtering and bucket collapse.

## References

Ortega, L. (2018). Lattice sieves for imaginary quantum workspaces. Journal of Speculative Computation, 12(4), 201-227.

Helix Research Group. (2022). Mirror sieves and coherence margins. Fictional Press.

title: How I Built a Fake Quantum Sieve Demo in a Weekend
html:
# How I Built a Fake Quantum Sieve Demo in a Weekend

I did not actually build a quantum computer. I built a story about one, because eval harnesses need paragraphs with personality.

The goal was simple: prove that my local search stack could retrieve a blog post when I asked navigational questions like that article about my weekend project.

## Motivation

Personal knowledge tools fail quietly. You only notice when you ask a reasonable question and get an irrelevant snippet about something you read three months ago.

So I fabricated Helix Labs, invented Ortega lattices, and typed furiously until the word counter smiled.

## What worked

Chunk overlap helped. Sliding windows felt archaic but predictable, which is exactly what you want before you rewrite everything in PR 3.

I also learned that summaries matter even when they are truncated. The indexer wants a field; give it a field.

## What failed

Trying to sound like a real VC-backed launch announcement while also explaining cosine similarity was a mistake. Pick one audience.

## Lessons

Ship the harness before you ship the clever algorithm. Measure the baseline. Tell the truth about the number.

- Week 1: sketched bucket functions on paper
- Week 2: wired a fake IndexedDB and cried once
- Week 3: added semantic fusion weights nobody asked for
- Week 4: wrote twenty eval queries and called it science

If you read this in an interview, remember: the project is real, the quantum sieve is not.
